points.title: The problem
points.name: Televisions are kept for a decade
points.description:
A television isn't a phone that got bigger. People buy one and keep it for years, so the app has to feel the same on a set from 2015 as on one bought last week — on older browser engines and a fraction of the memory a laptop has. 
 The codebase carried its own history too: Angular, coupled to an older project, with a special case for every television that disagreed with the others.

points.title: The approach
points.name: Fewer special cases, then speed
points.description: Moving to React was the visible part. The more valuable one was removing the special cases: every branch kept alive for a single manufacturer is a bug that only ever reproduces in somebody else's living room.
quotes: A deliberate polyfill strategy rather than shipping everything everywhere
CSS and LESS workarounds where old engines disagree, isolated and documented
Rendering optimisation aimed at the slowest device, not the average one
Build tools and dependencies kept current so the old targets don't freeze the new work

points.title: The launch
points.name: A platform with no precedent
points.description: Amazon's Vega OS arrived with no precedent to lean on. I read the SDK, established what the platform would and wouldn't support, adapted the app and took it through to store submission — the whole path.

points.title: The team
points.name: Knowing what the devices will take
points.description:
Owning the platform means I'm in the room early, which is where I'm most useful: saying clearly that a good idea won't run, before it becomes a design somebody has to undo. 
 After release I watch it closely, fix what's ours, and give the support team a straight answer for everything that isn't.

data.title: Angular to React, in production
data.headline: Replaced in flight.
data.summary: Moving a long-lived app onto React while it kept shipping every few weeks. A story about sequencing more than speed.
data.intro: Filmin's TV app was Angular, coupled to an older project, carrying years of special cases. It became fully React without a release freeze — the app kept shipping while the framework changed underneath it.

smart_tags.name: Legacy debt
smart_tags.description: Duplicated platform logic consolidated

points.title: The problem
points.name: A rewrite nobody can pause for
points.description:
The safe way to change frameworks is to stop everything else and do only that. A streaming service can't: features, device certifications and fixes keep their own calendar. The migration had to happen inside the normal release rhythm, or not at all. 
 The codebase made it harder — Angular coupled to an older project, and a special case for every television that disagreed with the rest.

points.title: The approach
points.name: Sequence over speed
points.description: Decouple first, so the app stood on its own. Then move it piece by piece, with both frameworks running in the same build until the last Angular view was gone. Consolidating the platform special cases as each piece crossed over meant the React side started cleaner than the Angular side had ever been.
quotes: Decoupled from the legacy project before touching the UI
Migrated incrementally, both frameworks coexisting in the build
Platform-specific branches consolidated as they crossed over
Old targets still supported — Chrome 23 didn't move

points.title: The result
points.name: One hundred percent, quietly
points.description: Angular is retired. One React codebase ships to every device at once, and the effort that used to go into keeping two worlds alive goes into the product instead.

points.title: The problem
points.name: Nothing to search for
points.description: Every mature platform comes with years of other people's mistakes to learn from. Vega came with an SDK and not much else — no answered questions, no institutional knowledge, nobody at the company who had shipped on it. The usual way of unblocking yourself didn't exist.

points.title: The approach
points.name: Read first, build second
points.description: Before adapting anything, I read the SDK and built a picture of what the platform would support and what our app assumed that Vega didn't provide. That map decided the work: what could stay, what needed adapting, what had to be raised with Amazon directly.
quotes: SDK evaluation before a line of app code
Capability map of what Vega would and wouldn't support
Adaptation of the existing React app, not a rewrite
A direct line to Amazon for what the docs didn't cover

data.headline: Every record stays with you.
data.summary: A personal finance app that keeps every record on the device. Design, build and release start to finish — product decisions included.
data.intro: A personal finance app with one rule: records live on the device and in the owner's own iCloud — no server of mine ever holds them. Designed, built, shipped and marketed by one person.

points.title: The problem
points.name: Finance apps ask for too much
points.description: The default trade in personal finance is convenience for custody: connect your bank, create an account, and a copy of your financial life lives on somebody's server. Crescia refuses the trade — records stay on the device and in the owner's own iCloud, and nowhere else.

points.title: The build
points.name: One person, every hat
points.description: SwiftUI and SwiftData underneath, iCloud as the only sync. The features that usually justify a server had to be solved without one.
quotes: Bank statement import, parsed with the Claude API
Subscriptions through StoreKit, tested in sandbox before anyone paid
An iOS widget for the home screen
SwiftData persistence, syncing through the owner's iCloud alone

points.title: The store
points.name: The part nobody warns you about
points.description: App Store Connect has its own curriculum: a monthly subscription rejected in review, a product ID reserved permanently by a mistake you can't undo, and the release cycles in between. The distance between writing an app and shipping one lives here.

points.title: The reach
points.name: Marketing is part of the product
points.description: A shipped app nobody finds is a side project. ASO across the Spanish and English listings, Instagram campaigns measured with funnel analysis, and a featuring nomination submitted to Apple.

points.title: The itch
points.name: A timer that minds its own business
points.description: Fasting trackers tend to arrive with accounts, streaks and a server watching. Yantar is the simple version: track the fast, keep the data on the phone, ask for nothing.

points.title: The build
points.name: Design as half the work
points.description: A tracker this small lives or dies on its interface — there's no feature list to hide behind. SwiftUI, and more hours in the design than the data model.

points.title: The lesson
points.name: What shipping teaches
points.description: The first full pass through App Store review, release and everything around it. What it taught carried straight into Crescia — which is the point of shipping a first app at all.

points.title: The context
points.name: Code with an audience of engineers
points.description: Building components other teams depend on changes the job. Your API is a promise, a breaking change is somebody else's incident, and 'it works on my product' isn't a standard. Stencil kept the widgets framework-agnostic so consuming teams weren't tied to our choices.

points.title: The migration
points.name: A public site, moved carefully
points.description: I led the migration of a legacy public-facing site to modern React, holding Jest coverage above 90% on the components I owned. In banking, coverage isn't a vanity metric — it's what lets a release go out without a week of manual checks.

points.title: The releases
points.name: Owning what happens after
points.description: Deployment and post-release bug resolution were mine, through Azure DevOps, in an environment where mistakes are visible to a lot of people very quickly. Shipping carefully became a habit rather than a policy.

points.title: The context
points.name: Four apps, small team
points.description: Two products, each needing a web app and a mobile app. In a team that size nobody stays neatly inside a job title — the work is whatever the product needs next.

points.title: The stack
points.name: Crossing the line, carefully
points.description: The front ends were mine: both web apps in React and TypeScript, both mobile apps in React Native, interfaces worked out with UI/UX in Figma. On the other side I contributed to the new Python and Django backend alongside the backend team — endpoint work, PostgreSQL queries, data through Django Admin. Their responsibility, my education.

points.title: The takeaway
points.name: Where full-stack started
points.description: Understanding both sides of the API changed how I write the client side — what to ask the server for, what to keep, what to never duplicate. That habit started here and never left.
